implementation_notes: A Go type definition is the pattern in the language: 'a type definition creates a new, distinct type with the same underlying type and operations as the given type', so UserID and string are different types, an OrderID does not satisfy a UserID parameter and every conversion is explicit. Methods can be attached to the defined type, which is where parsing, normalisation and formatting belong, so the classic wrapper struct is not needed at all - the distinct type plus a Parse function is the whole realization and it costs nothing at runtime. Reach for a struct instead only when the value needs more than one field (a unit plus an amount, for example), which is Value Object territory.
pitfalls: Conversions are explicit but always legal: UserID(anyString) compiles anywhere, so the type only distinguishes what the code does not convert - pair it with a validating constructor and keep the raw form out of signatures.
A defined type does not inherit the underlying type's methods, and %v prints the raw value: add a String() method if the value is a secret or needs formatting.
The zero value UserID("") is a valid instance, so 'absent' and 'empty' need an explicit representation (*UserID or a sentinel constant) rather than a bare empty string.
